teaser: Nails, a tram ticket, a rusty ring and the smallest word in German, promoted to art.

lesson.text: Hanover, Germany, 1919. Kurt Schwitters is 32, with a wife, a baby son and a room in his parents' house. The war has just been lost. The emperor has fled, there is fighting in the streets, food is rationed and money is starting to lose its value. Good paint and canvas are luxuries.

Schwitters had spent the end of the war as a technical draftsman in an ironworks, drawing machine parts. Now he walks the city with his eyes on the pavement and fills his pockets: tickets, wrappers, bits of wood, lids, wire. At home, he nails and glues them to a board.

lesson.title: The inventory
lesson.text: Four of the things he picked up and kept.

spots.title: und
spots.text: Three fat black letters cut from a printed sheet, probably an advertisement or poster. They are the largest, loudest thing here, and they gave the work its name.

spots.title: A machine part
spots.text: A dark toothed piece of metal, fixed right onto the surface. The former draftsman of machine parts now uses a real one, broken and useless.

spots.title: An address
spots.text: A printed strip: E. Sökeland & Söhne, Berlin N.W. 21. A real company, from a letterhead or a parcel label. Business mail turned into a band of pale color.

spots.title: The ring
spots.text: A heavy dark ring, like a rusted hoop or a horseshoe bent round. It sticks out from the surface, so the picture casts real shadows.

lesson.text: “Und” simply means “and”. The title, Das Undbild, is “The And-Picture”. Schwitters picked the humblest word in the language, the one nobody notices, and put it where a saint or a king would once have gone. It also describes his method: this and this and this.

Schwitters called everything he made “Merz”. The word means nothing. He cut it out of an advertisement for the Kommerz und Privatbank, a commercial bank, liked the sound, and kept it as the name of his art for the rest of his life.

He needed his own label because nobody else would have him. The Dada artists in Berlin, who also made angry art from scraps, turned down his request to join their club. Too middle-class, they felt, too fond of beauty. So Schwitters became a movement with a single member.

They had a point about beauty. Schwitters had trained as a painter at the academy in Dresden, and it shows. His rubbish is not thrown down. It is placed, turned and balanced as carefully as the apples in a still life.
Take away the objects and three big shapes hold everything in place.

lines.label: The blue wedge
lines.text: The only strong cool color, right of center, pointing down like a blade. Every warm brown and ochre around it looks warmer by contrast.

lines.label: The white arc
lines.text: A large pale shape swells along the left side like a sail. Its curve softens a picture made mostly of sharp corners.

lines.label: The slide
lines.text: In the lower half, strips and labels all tilt the same way, down to the right. The slope sets the heap in motion, as if it were still settling.

lesson.text: Those shapes are not only cut paper. Schwitters brushed paint over and between his scraps: the white of the arc, the blue of the wedge, the dark corner at top right. Paint is the glue for the eye. It ties a tram ticket to a piece of tin so they read as one surface.

The whole thing is barely bigger than a sheet of office paper, about 36 by 28 cm (14 by 11 in). Several pieces are held on with nails, and you can see the round heads here and there, especially along the Berlin address strip.

Your brain will try to read it. That is a reflex: show us letters and we look for sense. Schwitters knew this and played against it. He chops words in half, tilts them, and in one case turns the print on its head.
One printed slip, with a large number on it, is glued upside down. Where?

spots.title: The flipped slip
spots.text: Top left corner: an orange printed slip with a big 2, pasted the wrong way up. Unreadable at a glance, it stops being information and becomes a patch of orange with black marks.

lesson.text: That is the quiet shock of Merz. A ticket, once used, is worth nothing. An address is only useful to a postman. Freed from their jobs, they turn out to have color, texture and weight. In a country where everything had broken, Schwitters built from the pieces.

The same year, Schwitters became famous for a poem, not a picture. “An Anna Blume”, a nonsense love poem to a girl whose name reads the same forward and backward, was pasted on walls in Hanover and argued about across Germany.

spots.text: Two big printed numerals, half hidden under a strip of wood. A house number, a price, a page? Cut loose from its context, it is just a pair of handsome black curves.

spots.title: The splinter
spots.text: A flat pointed piece of wood, laid across like a compass needle. It throws a thin real shadow on the white paint beneath.

spots.title: A small disc
spots.text: A round metal piece like a button or washer, fixed at its center. A smaller cousin of the toothed part below it.

spots.title: Broken words
spots.text: Heavy old-fashioned German lettering on an orange band, sliced off mid-word. You can make out letters but no message.

spots.title: The little box
spots.text: A small tray with compartments and dark lumps inside, at the bottom edge. Schwitters leaves it unexplained, like a find at the back of a drawer.

spots.title: A paper label
spots.text: A yellowed printed label with fine type and a number, tilted on its side. The kind of paper that passes through a hand once and is thrown away.

lesson.text: Schwitters proved that what a work is made of does not decide its worth. What counts is the choosing and the placing.

The Nazis later mocked his work as “degenerate”, and he fled, first to Norway, then to England. A whole house interior he had built from scraps in Hanover was destroyed by bombs in 1943. He died in 1948, poor and little known. A few years on, artists like Robert Rauschenberg were filling canvases with street junk, and the And-Picture began to look like a beginning.

quiz.question: What does “und” mean?
quiz.explanation: It is the German word for “and”, which gives the work its title, The And-Picture.

quiz.question: Where did the word “Merz” come from?
options: A scrap of an advertisement for the Kommerz und Privatbank
quiz.explanation: He cut the syllable out of a bank advertisement and kept it.

quiz.question: How did the Berlin Dada group respond to Schwitters?
options: They refused to let him join
quiz.explanation: They turned him down, so he worked under his own label.

quiz.question: What ties the separate scraps together visually?
options: A sheet of glass over the top
Paint brushed over and between them
quiz.explanation: Schwitters painted across his materials so they read as one surface.

quiz.question: What made Schwitters famous in 1919?
options: A nonsense love poem called “An Anna Blume”
quiz.explanation: The poem was pasted on walls and debated across Germany.

quiz.question: What job did Schwitters do at the end of the war?
quiz.explanation: He drew machine parts, and later used a real metal part in this work.

facts.text: Das Undbild is a large mural covering a whole wall.
facts.explanation: It is small, about 36 by 28 cm, close to a sheet of office paper.

facts.text: Some of the objects are fixed to the board with nails.
facts.explanation: Nail heads are visible, especially along the Berlin address strip.

facts.text: Schwitters was a self-taught artist with no formal training.
facts.explanation: He studied painting at the academy in Dresden.
